dispute.reason: The 2012 IBSF World Billiards Championship in Leeds featured two separate official formats: the Points Format (150-Up), won by Rupesh Shah (Option B), and the Timed Format, won by Pankaj Advani (Option D). Because the question stem asks generically who won the "World Billiard Championship, 2012" without specifying the format, both Option B and Option D are factually world champions of 2012. Commercial keys that unilaterally keyed Option D ignored the Points Format champion. The question cannot be resolved to a single key and should remain unkeyed or unscored.

explanation.correct_reasoning: The International Billiards & Snooker Federation (IBSF) conducted two separate world championship disciplines in Leeds in October 2012: the Points Format (150-Up), won by Rupesh Shah (Option B), and the Timed Format (Long Format), won by Pankaj Advani (Option D). Because the question stem omitted the format qualification, both Option B and Option D are factually defensible world championship winners from the same official event. Third-party commercial keys typically print Pankaj Advani (D), but the question is formally defective as a single-choice question.

option_explanations.reason: Mike Russell (England) was a nine-time world billiards champion and reached the final of the 2012 IBSF World Billiards Championship (Timed Format) in Leeds, England, but lost in the final to Pankaj Advani (1895–1216). He was the runner-up and did not win the 2012 championship title.

Rupesh Shah (India) won the 2012 IBSF World Billiards Championship in the Points Format (150-Up), defeating Australia's Matthew Bolton 6–2 in the final on October 24, 2012 at the Northern Snooker Centre in Leeds. Because the question stem asks generically who won the "World Billiard Championship, 2012" without specifying the format, Rupesh Shah is an independently verified 2012 world champion.

Dhruv Sitwala (India) was an elite international cueist and multi-time Asian and World Billiards finalist/medallist, but he did not win the 2012 IBSF World Billiards Championship in either the Points or Timed format.

Pankaj Advani (India) won the 2012 IBSF World Billiards Championship in the Timed Format, defeating Mike Russell 1895–1216 in the final on October 28, 2012 at the Northern Snooker Centre in Leeds. Because the question stem does not specify whether the points format or timed format was intended, Pankaj Advani is an independently verified 2012 world champion.

Independent audit of MPPSC's official Final Answer Key (Vigyapti No. 583/Exam/2021) confirms that the dispute was formally resolved by the Commission by officially accepting both Option A ("Tantia") and Option D ("Tandra"). Colonial judicial records document Tantia while vernacular tribal history documents Tandra; both answers are historically authentic.
dispute.raised_by: Independent Research Audit / MPPSC Final Answer Key Revision

explanation.correct_reasoning: Tantya Bhil (c. 1842–1889) was the legendary tribal freedom fighter and folk hero of the Nimar region. In British archival, police, and judicial records of the Central Provinces (including his 1889 trial at Jabalpur), his name was recorded as "Tantia". Concurrently, regional tribal folklore and MP state publications document his original birth name as "Tandra". While MPPSC's provisional key initially marked Option A alone, the Commission's Final Answer Key (Vigyapti No. 583/Exam/2021) officially accepted BOTH Option A ("Tantia") and Option D ("Tandra"). Both options are historically authenticated.

option_explanations.reason: Colonial court and police records—specifically the 1889 Jabalpur Central Jail trial documents, British Central Provinces gazettes, and warrants—consistently recorded his official legal name as "Tantia" (or "Tantiya" / "Tautia"). MPPSC's Final Answer Key officially accepted Option A as correct.
Ganapat (Ganpat) was the name of a relative/associate in historical narratives of Tantya Bhil's circle in the Nimar/Khandwa region, not Tantya Bhil's own personal or given name.
Bijania (Bijaniya) was the name of another Bhil resistance fighter and associate operating in the Satpura/Nimar hills, not Tantya Bhil's given name.

In regional tribal oral tradition, Nimar folklore, and authoritative historical monographs published by the Madhya Pradesh Hindi Granth Academy and the Tribal Welfare Department, Tantya Bhil's childhood/given birth name is recorded as "Tandra" (टांड्रा or तांद्रा), from which "Tantia"/"Tantya" later evolved. Following candidate objections backed by regional historical documentation, MPPSC's Final Answer Key explicitly accepted Option D as correct alongside Option A.

key_concepts: Tantya Bhil (Krantisurya / Indian Robin Hood) - 19th-century tribal revolutionary from Nimar
Regional tribal oral history and Hindi Granth Academy documenting "Tandra"
MPPSC 2020 Final Answer Key revision adopting dual keys (A and D)
revision_takeaways: Both "Tantia" (official/colonial archival spelling) and "Tandra" (indigenous given name) were officially accepted by MPPSC in the 2020 Final Key.

dispute.reason: Jayaprakash Narayan systematically formulated the doctrine of "Partyless Democracy" in his 1959 work "A Plea for the Reconstruction of Indian Polity". Mahatma Gandhi laid the philosophical foundation in January 1948 by proposing that the Congress disband as a political party to become a non-partisan Lok Sevak Sangh. Because both thinkers prominently proposed eliminating political parties from democratic governance in India, MPPSC's Final Answer Key officially accepted both C and D. Both options are intellectually defensible.
dispute.raised_by: Independent Research Audit / MPPSC Final Answer Key Revision

explanation.correct_reasoning: The political doctrine of "Partyless Democracy" was formally coined, formulated, and published by Jayaprakash Narayan (Option D) in "A Plea for the Reconstruction of Indian Polity" (1959) and revitalized during his 1974 Total Revolution. However, Mahatma Gandhi (Option C) provided the ideological foundation for party-free Indian democracy in his January 1948 draft proposing the dissolution of the Congress as a political party into a non-partisan Lok Sevak Sangh. Because both thinkers prominently proposed eliminating political parties from democratic governance in India, MPPSC's Final Answer Key officially accepted both C and D.

option_explanations.reason: Shripad Amrit Dange was a founding leader of the Communist Party of India (CPI) and a prominent trade unionist. He advocated working within a vanguard party and parliamentary/mass party politics, rather than abolishing political parties.

Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia was a socialist thinker who fiercely opposed Congress hegemony and proposed the "Four-Pillar State" (Chaukhamba Raj) and militant socialist politics, but he operated through and built distinct political parties (Socialist Party, Samyukta Socialist Party), not a partyless system.

On January 29–30, 1948, Mahatma Gandhi authored his "Last Will and Testament" (published in Harijan on February 15, 1948), proposing that the Indian National Congress had outlived its role as a propaganda vehicle and political party and should disband to transform into a "Lok Sevak Sangh"—a non-partisan association of social servants working for village swaraj outside the party system. Because this proposal represents the foundational Indian argument against party-based competitive politics, MPPSC officially accepted Option C as correct.

Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) formulated and popularized the specific political doctrine of "Partyless Democracy" (दलविहीन प्रजातंत्र / Lokniti) in his 1959 treatise "A Plea for the Reconstruction of Indian Polity" and during the 1974 Total Revolution (Sampoorna Kranti). JP argued that party competition fragmented village communities and created self-serving oligarchies, advocating instead for participatory grassroots democracy through village assemblies. MPPSC officially accepted Option D as correct.

A Plea for the Reconstruction of Indian Polity (Sarva Seva Sangh, 1959)
Mahatma Gandhi's 1948 Last Will and Testament: Lok Sevak Sangh proposal
Decentralized Panchayati Raj vs competitive party electoral machinery
revision_takeaways: Jayaprakash Narayan is the definitive theorist of "Partyless Democracy"; Mahatma Gandhi was its philosophical precursor. MPPSC officially accepts both C and D.

dispute.reason: The dedicated sports award conferred by the Madhya Pradesh Government on a coach is the Vishwamitra Award (instituted 1994, conferred from 1995–96 onwards). The four printed options name Dronacharya (Central Govt), Parashuram (Himachal Pradesh Govt), Vikram (MP award for senior athletes), and Sandipani (educational/non-sports). Because the only correct award—the Vishwamitra Award—was omitted from all four options, no option is correct. The question is defective and must remain unkeyed and unscored.

explanation.correct_reasoning: The official sports award given by the Madhya Pradesh Government to a coach for outstanding dedication and mentorship is the Vishwamitra Award (विश्वामित्र पुरस्कार), instituted in 1994 (rules notified in 1994 and conferred from 1995–96 onwards) by the Department of Sports and Youth Welfare. The Dronacharya Award (A) is a national award of the Government of India; the Parashuram Award (B) is a sports award of Himachal Pradesh; the Vikram Award (C) is an MP award for senior players, not coaches; and no Sandipani sports award exists (D). Because the only correct award—the Vishwamitra Award—was omitted from all four options, this question is intrinsically defective and contains no correct answer.

option_explanations.reason: The Dronacharya Award is indeed an honour for sports coaches, but it is conferred by the Central Government of India (Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, instituted 1985), not by the Madhya Pradesh State Government.
The Parashuram (Parshuram) Award is the highest state sports award conferred by the Government of Himachal Pradesh (instituted 1987). It is not an award of the Madhya Pradesh Government.
The Vikram Award is conferred by the Madhya Pradesh Government (instituted 1990), but it is the highest state honour reserved strictly for senior players/athletes, not for coaches.

There is no sports coaching award named Sandipani Award under the Madhya Pradesh Department of Sports and Youth Welfare. Sandipani is associated with Vedic education institutions in Ujjain and state school schemes.
